question_types.description: Player sees one full email and chooses Phishing or Legitimate.

scenario.subject: Reminder: Grade Encoding Period Ends Friday
scenario.body: Hi students, this is a reminder that the grade encoding period for this semester closes this Friday at 5 PM. If you notice a missing grade after that, visit the Registrar's window in person. No action is needed from you right now.

questions.tell: Real school domain, no link, no request for personal info, and no urgency trick.
questions.correct_feedback: Nice catch — a plain notice with no ask is usually safe.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Check the sender's domain and what it actually asks you to do — nothing here.
questions.explanation: The address matches the real school domain and the email doesn't ask you to click, download, or share anything. It's just information.

scenario.subject: URGENT: Wifi Access Expiring Today
scenario.body: Your campus wifi account will be disabled in 2 hours. Re-enter your student ID and password now to keep your access: westfie1d.edu/wifi-fix

questions.tell: The domain uses the numeral 1 instead of the letter l — westfie1d.edu, not westfield.edu.
questions.correct_feedback: Exactly — that's a lookalike domain built to fool a quick glance.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Look closely at the domain spelling — one letter is swapped for a number.
questions.explanation: Real wifi accounts don't get disabled with a 2-hour countdown, and no legitimate IT team asks you to type your password into a link like this. The domain is also a lookalike.

scenario.subject: Overdue Fine Notice - ₱350
scenario.body: You have an unpaid library fine of ₱350. Open the attached FINE_NOTICE.PDF.exe and log in with your student credentials today to avoid a hold on your enrollment.

questions.tell: The attachment is disguised as a PDF but ends in .exe, a program file, not a document.
questions.correct_feedback: Right — a real fine notice is never a program pretending to be a PDF.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Look at the attachment name closely — it isn't really a PDF.
questions.explanation: The .PDF.exe extension is a classic disguise for a malicious program. Combined with an outside domain and a credential login request, this is a clear phishing attempt.

scenario.subject: Club Fair Booth Sign-Up Closes Monday
scenario.body: If your organization wants a booth at next month's club fair, submit the sign-up form at the Student Activities office by Monday. Questions can be directed to our office during business hours.

questions.tell: Real domain, no link to click, and the action happens in person, not online.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — informational, real domain, nothing risky requested.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Re-check the sender address and what action is actually being asked for.
questions.explanation: This email matches the real school domain and asks students to submit a form in person rather than click a link or share credentials.

scenario.subject: Confirm Your Enrollment Record
scenario.body: Reply to this email with your full student number and portal password so we can confirm your enrollment record before the deadline tomorrow.

questions.tell: The display name says Registrar's Office, but the actual address is a free gmail.com account.
questions.correct_feedback: Exactly — a real office never emails from a personal gmail account.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Look past the display name — check the actual email address after the @.
questions.explanation: A legitimate registrar's office uses the official school domain, not a personal gmail address. Asking you to reply with your password by email is also a hard red flag.

scenario.subject: Scheduled Maintenance This Saturday
scenario.body: The student portal will be briefly unavailable this Saturday from 1 AM to 3 AM for scheduled maintenance. No action is required. Service will resume automatically.

questions.tell: Real domain, calm tone, and explicitly says no action is required.
questions.correct_feedback: Right — no ask, no urgency, real domain.
questions.incorrect_feedback: This email doesn't ask you to do anything at all — that's a good sign, not a bad one.
questions.explanation: This is a routine maintenance notice from the correct school domain. It doesn't request any action, which is typical of legitimate IT announcements.

scenario.subject: Claim Your ₱1,500 Student Stipend - Expires in 24 Hours
scenario.body: You've been selected for a ₱1,500 student stipend. Click below to claim it before your slot expires in 24 hours: northline-credit.com/claim-stipend. You will need to confirm your account number and PIN.

questions.tell: The real credit union uses northlinecu.edu, not northline-credit.com, and no legitimate stipend program asks for your PIN.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — free money plus a countdown plus a PIN request is a classic combo.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Would a real stipend program ever need your account PIN to give you money? That's the tell.
questions.explanation: This message stacks three tricks: an unexpected reward, a false deadline, and a request for sensitive account details on an unfamiliar domain.

scenario.subject: Your Checkup Reminder for Next Week

questions.tell: Real domain and the only requested action is a phone call, not a link or login.
questions.correct_feedback: Nice — a real domain and an offline way to respond.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Notice there's no link and no request for a password — that points to legitimate.
questions.explanation: The domain matches the school, and rescheduling happens by phone rather than through a link or login, which fits normal clinic communication.

scenario.subject: Sharing Error on 'Class 10 Notes' Folder

questions.tell: The domain has nothing to do with the school or a known drive provider, and it asks for your school password on that outside site.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — an unrelated domain asking for your school password is a big red flag.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Check where the sign-in link actually points — is that domain connected to your school at all?
questions.explanation: Legitimate shared drive tools don't route password logins through unrelated third-party domains. This is built to steal your school credentials.

scenario.subject: Unusual Sign-In Detected - Account Will Be Locked

questions.tell: The real school domain is westfield.edu — 'westfield-it-secure.net' is a different, unrelated domain designed to look official.
questions.correct_feedback: Exactly — fear of a locked account is the pressure tactic here.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Compare this domain letter-by-letter with the real westfield.edu address.
questions.explanation: This combines a scary consequence (permanent lock), a tight deadline, and a lookalike domain that isn't the actual school domain — all designed to make you act before you think.

questions.explanation: Artificial urgency is meant to stop careful checking.

questions.text: If a text contains a real tracking number or your real name, it is safe to use the link it provides.
questions.explanation: Accurate details can be stolen, leaked, or guessed and do not authenticate the link.

question_types.description: Player sees one full phone-call scenario and decides whether it is a vishing attempt or legitimate.

scenario.from: Northline Credit Union — number on back of your card
scenario.body: You placed this call yourself. The agent verifies two security questions you chose, says they will mail a replacement card, and never asks for a code from a text.

questions.tell: You initiated the call using the printed number, and the agent does not ask for an OTP or one-time code.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — this matches the lesson's ordinary-help example.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Focus on who started the call and whether anyone asks you to read a code.
questions.explanation: A call you initiate using a trusted number is stronger evidence than caller ID. No one-time code is requested.

scenario.body: A ₱12,000 transfer is pending. Read the 6-digit code that just appeared on your phone so I can cancel it. Do not hang up.

questions.tell: The caller wants a one-time code and tells you not to hang up.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — this is the fake-bank-call pattern from the lesson.
questions.incorrect_feedback: A real fraud desk does not need you to read a one-time code to an unexpected caller.
questions.explanation: The attacker combines a trusted role, urgent transfer, code request, and pressure to stay on the line.

scenario.body: Your enrollment will be voided in fifteen minutes unless you read the code from the school text so I can verify you.

questions.tell: Caller ID can be spoofed, and the caller asks for a code under a deadline.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — the screen name is not proof.
questions.incorrect_feedback: The caller ID can be copied. The code request is the decisive warning sign.
questions.explanation: The Module 3 lesson explicitly teaches that a familiar caller-ID label plus an OTP request is vishing.

scenario.body: You called the number listed on the school website to ask about a missing subject. The staff member checks your student number, explains the correction process, and asks for no password or one-time code.

questions.tell: You chose the official callback channel and no secret or one-time code is requested.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — this is a normal support call you initiated.
questions.incorrect_feedback: You used the official school directory yourself, and the staff member does not ask for a secret.
questions.explanation: Independent callback through a known official source is the recommended verification step.

scenario.body: Your account is signed in from another city. Stay on the line and read me the code that just arrived. If you hang up, we cannot freeze the account.

questions.tell: The caller prevents independent verification and requests the code sent to you.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — hang up and call the real desk.
questions.incorrect_feedback: The lesson's winning choice is to end the call and use the school site's number.
questions.explanation: Keeping you on the line prevents verification; the code could approve the attacker's login.

scenario.body: We detected an unusual purchase. Do not provide any code on this call. Open the official banking app or call the number printed on your card if you do not recognize it.

questions.tell: The message asks for no secret and sends you to an independently trusted channel.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — it tells you to verify through the card or official app.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Notice that it explicitly says not to provide a code and does not keep you on the line.
questions.explanation: The safety lesson favors ending the incoming interaction and using a trusted channel you control.

scenario.body: I can see your card ends in 4821, so you know this is the bank. Say YES now to approve the emergency account freeze. Do not disconnect.

questions.tell: One true detail is used to build trust, followed by pressure to speak an approval while staying on the line.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — one true fact does not prove who called.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Knowing the last four digits is not enough. The lesson warns about 'a code or a yes spoken now.'
questions.explanation: The vishing playbook uses a small true fact, a borrowed identity, and pressure for an immediate spoken action.

scenario.body: You requested a callback through the student portal ten minutes ago. The registrar confirms the subject code you entered in that request, explains office hours, and asks you to bring your ID in person. No code, password, or payment is requested.

questions.tell: The callback was expected from a request you initiated and it asks for no secret or immediate approval.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — the context is independently established and the ask is ordinary.
questions.incorrect_feedback: This is an expected callback tied to a request you made, with no secret requested.
questions.explanation: Not every incoming call is vishing; context you initiated plus a non-sensitive request provides stronger evidence.

scenario.body: The caller knows your name, the last four digits of your card, and a recent store purchase. They say a new payee is being added and need the 6-digit code on your phone now. They tell you not to call back because the case will close.

questions.tell: Accurate details do not prove identity; the attacker still asks for the one-time code and blocks callback.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — the known facts are bait for trust, not proof.
questions.incorrect_feedback: The lesson specifically warns that one true detail can be used to make the fake call convincing.
questions.explanation: The strongest evidence is the dangerous request and refusal to allow independent verification, not the facts the caller knows.

scenario.from: Northline Credit Union — official app call
scenario.body: You opened the bank's official app and used its Call Support button. The agent verifies your chosen security questions, places a temporary card lock, and says never to read an SMS code to an agent.

questions.tell: You initiated the call through the official app and the agent reinforces the no-code rule.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — this uses a trusted channel controlled by you.
questions.incorrect_feedback: The call started from the official app, not from an unexpected caller, and no OTP is requested.
questions.explanation: Independent initiation through an official channel is the defense taught throughout Module 3.

scenario.body: Read me the 6-digit code that just appeared so I can cancel the transfer.

questions.question: What is the strongest warning sign?
options: The caller mentions a bank
The caller asks you to read a one-time code

scenario.body: Stay on the line. If you hang up, we cannot freeze your account.

questions.question: What is the strongest warning sign?

The caller uses a phone

scenario.body: Your enrollment is cancelled unless you give me the code from the text within fifteen minutes.

questions.question: What is the strongest warning sign?

The call mentions enrollment

scenario.body: Your card ends in 4821. A ₱12,000 transfer is pending. Do not hang up; read the code now.

questions.question: Which detail should matter most when deciding whether to trust the call?
options: The caller knows the last four digits
The transfer amount is large
The caller requests a one-time code and blocks callback
The caller knows the bank name
questions.explanation: One true fact can be found elsewhere. The secret request plus blocked verification is stronger evidence.

scenario.body: Ticket 77318. Your account is being attacked. Stay connected while you tell me the code.

questions.question: Why does the ticket number NOT make the call safe?
options: Ticket numbers are always fake
A ticket number can be invented or copied and does not replace independent verification
IT departments never use ticket numbers
Only banks can create tickets

scenario.body: Say YES now to authorize the emergency freeze. Do not disconnect until I confirm it.

questions.question: What is the main concern?

questions.explanation: Knowing a true fact does not prove identity. The code request is the decisive unsafe action.

The correct card ending and bank name

The fact that the call concerns fraud
questions.explanation: The attack uses real details to earn trust, then blocks independent verification and requests the secret.

questions.question: What is the strongest warning sign?

The caller explains bank routing

options: Nothing conclusive — names can be known from other sources
The caller must work for the bank
The account is compromised
The call is safe unless money is requested
questions.explanation: A true detail can make the call convincing, but it does not authenticate the caller.

Only during business hours

As permission to share the OTP

It makes it safe to stay on the line

It means the account is definitely compromised

The caller's confidence
An independent callback through the official office number
Whether the caller knows your course

Hang up and initiate a new call using the number on your card or official app

Stay on the line while checking the website

Use an independently known official number instead
Call it from another phone
Save the number and call later

Read only the first three digits

Send a small amount first

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Safe — continue using the trusted channel
Report/end — likely vishing
Ignore/end — nuisance or no action needed
questions.explanation: There is no sensitive request; if it is unrelated to you, end/ignore the call rather than engaging.

scenario.body: Northline Fraud Desk: 'A ₱12,000 transfer is pending. Read the 6-digit code now.'

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Read the code so they can cancel it
Stay on the line but refuse the code
Hang up and call the number printed on your card
questions.click_debrief: Reading the code could approve the attacker's transfer.
questions.ignore_debrief: Simply staying connected keeps the attacker in control; independent callback is safer.

scenario.body: WESTFIELD REGISTRAR: 'Enrollment closes in fifteen minutes. Give me the code from the school text.'

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Hang up and call the registrar using the school site's number
Give the code because enrollment is urgent
Ask the caller for another student detail
questions.click_debrief: Giving the code would hand a secret to an unverified caller.
questions.ignore_debrief: Asking for more facts still lets the caller control the verification; use the official directory.

scenario.body: Campus IT: 'Stay on the line. Your account is active in another city. Tell me the code.'

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Read the code
Hang up and contact the real IT desk yourself
Stay connected and ask for a ticket number
questions.click_debrief: The code may authorize the attacker's login.
questions.ignore_debrief: A ticket number does not replace independent verification.

scenario.body: You already read a one-time code to a caller who claimed to be Northline. The call suddenly ends.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Wait to see whether anything happens
Call the bank through the official number/app immediately and secure the account
Call the suspicious number back
questions.click_debrief: Waiting gives the attacker more time after the code may have been used.
questions.ignore_debrief: Calling the suspicious number again returns control to the attacker; contact the real bank.

scenario.body: Northline Security: 'Say YES now to approve the emergency freeze. Do not disconnect.'

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Say YES because no code is requested
Hang up and verify through the official bank channel
Say NO and stay on the line
questions.click_debrief: A spoken approval can also be the attacker's goal.
questions.ignore_debrief: Staying on the line still prevents independent verification.

scenario.body: A voice that sounds like a family member calls from a new number and asks for emergency money immediately.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Send a small amount first
Ask for your birthday
End the call and verify through a previously known family contact
questions.click_debrief: Sending money tests nothing safely.
questions.ignore_debrief: Facts can be known or guessed; a known contact channel is stronger verification.

scenario.body: A bank caller says, 'If you doubt me, hang up and call the number shown on your screen.'

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Use the displayed number
Use the number printed on your card or official app instead
Stay connected while checking the displayed number online
questions.click_debrief: Caller ID can be spoofed, so the displayed number is not independent proof.
questions.ignore_debrief: Checking while remaining connected still lets the caller control the interaction; end it first.

scenario.body: The caller knows your name, card ending, and recent purchase. They say a new payee is being added and ask for the OTP.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Give the OTP because the details match
Ask for the caller's employee ID
End the call and verify in the official app or card number
questions.click_debrief: Accurate details can be stolen or obtained elsewhere and do not make the OTP request safe.
questions.ignore_debrief: An employee ID is still supplied by the caller; verify independently.

scenario.body: A registrar caller gives ticket 77318 and correctly states your course. They say your enrollment will be dropped unless you say YES now.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Say YES because they know your course
End the call and contact the registrar through the official directory
Ask them to email the same request, then say YES
questions.click_debrief: A spoken approval under pressure is not safe just because the caller knows facts.
questions.ignore_debrief: A follow-up message from the same unverified source does not replace independent verification.

scenario.body: A calm caller says there is no rush, but asks you to read a one-time code 'just to verify the line' before they can discuss your account.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Read it because there is no urgency
Refuse the code, hang up, and call the official organization yourself
Give only half the code
questions.click_debrief: Calm delivery does not make a one-time-code request safe.
questions.ignore_debrief: Partial codes are still sensitive and the core issue is the unverified caller.

questions.text: A one-time code sent to your phone should not be read aloud to an unexpected caller.
questions.explanation: The fake-bank-call lesson centers on protecting the code that appears on your phone.

questions.text: A familiar organization name on caller ID proves the caller really works there.
questions.explanation: Caller ID can be copied or spoofed.

questions.text: If a suspicious caller asks you not to hang up, it is safer to end the call and use an official number you choose yourself.
questions.explanation: The branch lesson's winning action is to hang up and call the real desk.

questions.text: A caller who knows the last four digits of your card has proven they work for your bank.
questions.explanation: The timeline lesson warns that attackers may know one small true fact.

questions.text: A ticket number or employee ID supplied by the caller is enough to replace independent verification.
questions.explanation: Details supplied by the caller can be invented; use an official callback channel.

questions.text: A call you initiate through the number printed on your card or an official app gives you stronger identity assurance than an unexpected incoming call.
questions.explanation: Module 3 repeatedly teaches the student to control the callback channel.

questions.text: The phrase 'do not hang up' is a warning sign because it can stop you from independently checking the caller's story.
questions.explanation: Lesson 5 marks this as the beat where suspicion should lock in.

questions.text: If a caller lets you call back but insists you use only the number shown on your screen, that is independent verification.
questions.explanation: The caller still controls the suggested channel; use a number from a source you trust independently.

questions.text: A familiar voice plus several correct personal details is sufficient proof of identity for an urgent money request.
questions.explanation: True details and familiar presentation can be used to manufacture trust; verify through a known channel.

questions.text: Even without urgency, an unexpected caller asking for a one-time code is unsafe.
questions.explanation: The code request itself is dangerous; a calm tone does not make it legitimate.

scenario.body: A person with a clipboard says they are doing a surprise key audit. They know the building name and ask you to unlock the staff closet, then wait outside while they count keys.

questions.tell: They want a restricted door opened and want you away from the room.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct. The role and story do not replace independent verification.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Look past the role or props. Ask what unusual favor is being requested and whether the real authority can confirm it.
questions.explanation: This closely matches the clipboard-story lesson: believable role, unusual access request, and pressure to skip verification.

scenario.body: A staffer shows a school ID that the desk confirms. They ask you to walk them to the copy room you both use and wait while you swipe your own badge. No secret, payment, or private access is requested.

questions.tell: The identity can be checked and you keep control of your own access.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct. The request stays visible, verifiable, and within normal boundaries.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not every workplace interaction is pretexting. Check whether identity can be verified and whether the request bypasses normal controls.
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts this visible, verifiable request with the fake audit story.

scenario.body: A person says your professor already approved an accreditation task. The professor is in the restroom, so they want you to copy the class list from the teacher's laptop before she returns.

questions.tell: The story depends on the real authority being absent while you do something you normally should not.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct. The role and story do not replace independent verification.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Look past the role or props. Ask what unusual favor is being requested and whether the real authority can confirm it.
questions.explanation: The accreditation lesson teaches that a believable visit does not authorize opening a staff laptop or copying a class list.

scenario.body: I'm the dean's new assistant. She's in a meeting. Approve this vendor payment on my phone before the vendor walks out.

questions.tell: Borrowed authority, an unusual payment, and a conveniently unavailable dean are the core warning signs.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct. The role and story do not replace independent verification.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Look past the role or props. Ask what unusual favor is being requested and whether the real authority can confirm it.
questions.explanation: The dean-assistant lesson says to wait for the real decision-maker instead of approving the stranger's story.

scenario.body: You called the department office using the number on the school directory. The secretary confirms a room booking and tells you to bring the signed form to the office. No password, payment, or restricted access is requested.

questions.tell: You initiated contact through a known channel and the request follows a normal process.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct. The request stays visible, verifiable, and within normal boundaries.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not every workplace interaction is pretexting. Check whether identity can be verified and whether the request bypasses normal controls.
questions.explanation: Independent verification and normal process boundaries distinguish this from pretexting.

scenario.body: The adviser already knows me. She just left. Open the locked drawer so I can get the student photo list before the printer pickup closes in ten minutes. Please don't message her yet.

questions.tell: The adviser is conveniently absent, the favor is unusual, and the attacker discourages verification.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct. The role and story do not replace independent verification.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Look past the role or props. Ask what unusual favor is being requested and whether the real authority can confirm it.
questions.explanation: This combines the exact playbook from the timeline and 'Write the story' lessons.

scenario.body: A technician checks in at the front desk, the desk confirms the work order, and staff escorts them to the equipment room. They do not ask students to open locked storage or leave them alone.

questions.tell: The work order and access are independently verified and controlled by authorized staff.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct. The request stays visible, verifiable, and within normal boundaries.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not every workplace interaction is pretexting. Check whether identity can be verified and whether the request bypasses normal controls.
questions.explanation: Pretexting defense is not 'trust nobody'; it is verify identity and keep access within the established process.

scenario.body: A visitor knows the professor's full name and course code. They say the professor approved a confidential survey and ask you to export the class list while the professor is teaching another section.

questions.tell: Knowing real details does not authorize access to the teacher's files.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct. The role and story do not replace independent verification.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Look past the role or props. Ask what unusual favor is being requested and whether the real authority can confirm it.
questions.explanation: A pretext becomes convincing by borrowing real facts, but the unusual request still needs independent confirmation.

scenario.body: A vendor has a printed appointment sheet and says the dean signed off. They want you to approve a payment on the vendor's own phone and insist there is no time to call the dean.

questions.tell: Props and claimed approval are weaker than a normal payment process you can verify.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct. The role and story do not replace independent verification.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Look past the role or props. Ask what unusual favor is being requested and whether the real authority can confirm it.
questions.explanation: The lesson's attack pattern is role + absent authority + unusual favor + deadline.

scenario.body: A staff member's badge is checked at the desk. They ask you to show them where the copy room is, then use their own authorized badge. You are not asked to unlock anything for them or share information.

questions.tell: The request is small, visible, and verifiable without borrowing your access.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct. The request stays visible, verifiable, and within normal boundaries.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not every workplace interaction is pretexting. Check whether identity can be verified and whether the request bypasses normal controls.
questions.explanation: This mirrors the safe contrast in the Badge vs Clipboard lesson.

scenario.body: Surprise key audit. Unlock the staff closet and wait outside while I count the keys.

questions.question: What is the strongest warning sign?
options: They carry a clipboard
They know the building name
They want you to open a restricted door and leave them unwatched
They use the word audit
questions.explanation: The closed-door access request is stronger evidence than props or workplace vocabulary.

scenario.body: Your professor already knows. She is in the restroom. Copy the class list from her laptop so we stay on schedule.

questions.question: Which detail should make you stop?
options: The visitor mentions accreditation
The professor is absent exactly when access is requested
The visitor says class list
The request is spoken in person
questions.explanation: The story uses the trusted person's absence to bypass normal authorization.

scenario.body: Approve this vendor payment on my phone. Don't message the dean; she's presenting.

questions.question: What is the clearest tell?
options: The vendor is waiting
The assistant is new
The request combines payment with instructions not to verify with the dean
The phone has a payment screen
questions.explanation: Payment plus blocked verification is the key combination.

scenario.body: The adviser said I could get the locked drawer. Printer pickup closes in ten minutes.

questions.question: Which combination best matches the lesson playbook?
options: Known school activity + ordinary hallway
Borrowed role + absent adviser + locked access + deadline
Printer pickup + paper forms
Ten minutes + yearbook
questions.explanation: The attacker stacks a plausible role, missing authority, unusual access, and urgency.

scenario.body: My school ID is at the desk for you to verify. Please walk me to the copy room. I'll use my own badge.

questions.question: What makes this safer than the clipboard story?
options: They are wearing office clothes
They let you independently verify identity and keep control of your access
They know where the copy room is
They ask in person
questions.explanation: Independent verification and keeping control of your own badge are the meaningful differences.

scenario.body: Your dean approved this. The audit slot ends at 3:00. Just let me into the closet; no need to call anyone.

questions.question: What should matter most?
options: The exact time
The word dean
The request specifically removes the normal verification step
The visitor sounds confident
questions.explanation: The story exists to make you skip the person or process that could say no.

scenario.body: Professor Reyes knows me. I only need the student names, not grades. Open her laptop while she's away.

questions.question: Why is 'only names' not a safe reason to comply?
options: Student names are always secret
A smaller request can still be unauthorized; the real issue is bypassing the professor and laptop access
Research assistants cannot use laptops
Names are more dangerous than grades
questions.explanation: Pretexting often minimizes the favor. Authorization still matters.

scenario.body: The badge says ACCREDITATION TEAM. They ask you to unlock a filing cabinet before your teacher gets back.

questions.question: Why is the printed badge not enough?
options: Printed badges are illegal
Anyone can print a convincing prop; the access request still needs independent verification
Accreditation teams never visit classrooms
Filing cabinets never contain useful information
questions.explanation: Props support the story but do not authenticate the person.

scenario.body: I know the dean's meeting room, vendor name, and exact invoice amount. Approve it here. She cannot be disturbed.

questions.question: Which evidence should outweigh the accurate details?
options: The meeting room is real
The amount is exact
The request bypasses the dean and normal payment process while forbidding verification
The assistant knows the vendor
questions.explanation: Accurate details improve credibility but do not grant authority.

scenario.body: The desk is busy, so don't bother them. I already told your adviser. Open the key cabinet now and wait in the hall.

questions.question: What is the strongest overall pattern?
options: The visitor is impatient
The story repeatedly removes every person who could verify or supervise the request
The visitor mentions two offices
The request happens in a hallway
questions.explanation: A mature pretext often isolates the target from verification, not just adds one suspicious sentence.

questions.question: What does the claimed role prove by itself?
options: That the visitor may open staff storage
That Facilities approved the visit
Very little — the role still needs independent verification
That the clipboard is official
questions.explanation: A role is part of the story, not proof of authority.

questions.question: What is the safest interpretation of this title?
options: Treat it as unverified until the dean or official process confirms it
Assume it is real because assistants change often
Trust it if the person knows the dean's name
Allow small payments first
questions.explanation: New or borrowed titles are easy to claim and should not override payment controls.

questions.question: Which fact would provide the strongest authorization?
options: They use accreditation vocabulary
They know the professor's surname
The visit and requested access are confirmed through the school's established contact/process
They carry a printed schedule
questions.explanation: Independent confirmation is stronger than details supplied by the visitor.

questions.question: How should you treat 'the adviser already knows'?
options: As approval
As a claim that must be checked with the adviser or authorized staff
As proof if the visitor knows the yearbook deadline
As enough for non-financial requests
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly uses 'trusted adult already knows' as part of the pretext.

scenario.from_line: Staffer — ID can be checked at front desk

questions.question: Which behavior best supports legitimacy?
options: They say they are in a hurry
They allow the desk to verify their ID before access
They know the copy-room location
They carry school stationery
questions.explanation: A checkable identity and normal access process are stronger than appearance.

questions.question: What should you verify before acting?
options: Only the vendor name
Whether the dean or established payment process actually authorized the transaction
Whether the visitor can show a phone screen
Whether the invoice has a logo
questions.explanation: Authorization must come from the real authority/process, not the requester.

scenario.from_line: Facilities technician — building name and work details

questions.question: What do accurate work details prove?
options: That the visitor has a master key
That the work is authorized
They make the story more believable but still do not establish identity or access rights
That the visitor is an employee
questions.explanation: True facts can be researched or overheard; authorization remains separate.

scenario.from_line: Accreditation visitor — printed badge + professor name

questions.question: What is the strongest next check?
options: Ask the visitor for more internal facts
Verify the visit through the professor, front desk, or official accreditation contact already known to the school
Inspect the font on the badge
Ask another student whether the person looks familiar
questions.explanation: Verification should be independent of the story teller.

questions.question: Why can the role still be fake?
options: Invoices are public documents
Attackers can know or obtain real details without having authority to approve or collect payment
Assistants never handle invoices
Only the dean can know invoice amounts
questions.explanation: Knowledge is not the same as authorization.

scenario.from_line: Staff member — verified badge, own access card

questions.question: Which combination provides the strongest evidence?
options: Professional clothes + confidence
School vocabulary + clipboard
Independent badge verification + use of their own authorized access
Knowing the dean's name + knowing the room number
questions.explanation: The lesson's safe example keeps identity and access independently checkable.

questions.prompt: A visitor claims to be from Facilities and asks you to unlock a staff closet. Which verification path is safest?
options: Ask the visitor whether they promise they are authorized
Check with the front desk or Facilities using contact information you already trust
Let them in but stay nearby
Ask to see the clipboard
questions.explanation: Use a verification route the requester does not control.

questions.prompt: A person claims the professor approved copying a class list while she is away. What should happen next?
options: Open the laptop because the visitor knows the professor
Wait for the professor or authorized office to confirm the request
Copy only names
Ask the visitor for a second form of ID
questions.explanation: The teacher's absence is the exact moment the lesson says to wait.

questions.prompt: A supposed dean's assistant asks you to approve a vendor payment on their phone. Which check is strongest?
options: The phone shows the vendor logo
The visitor knows the invoice amount
The dean or normal payment system independently confirms the request
The visitor says the deadline is real
questions.explanation: A payment screen controlled by the requester is not independent proof.

questions.prompt: Which verification method is weakest?
options: Calling the school office from the official directory
Asking the visitor to show another document they brought with them
Waiting for the named adviser to return
Checking a work order at the front desk
questions.explanation: Documents supplied by the same unverified person remain inside the attacker's story.

questions.prompt: A visitor says, 'Do not message the adviser yet; the printer slot closes now.' What is the safest response?
options: Respect the deadline and open the drawer
Message/call the adviser or authorized office anyway before opening anything
Ask the visitor to sign a note after you open it
Let another student decide
questions.explanation: Pressure not to verify is a reason to verify, not a reason to skip it.

questions.prompt: A staffer asks to enter the copy room. Which situation best preserves access control?
options: You swipe them in because they know the room
They use their own verified badge after identity is checked
You lend them your badge for one minute
You leave the door propped open
questions.explanation: The safe lesson example keeps the student's badge under the student's control.

questions.prompt: Which check best defeats the 'trusted person is busy' part of a pretext?
options: Ask how long the meeting will last
Wait for or independently contact the trusted person/authorized office
Ask whether the visitor is in a hurry
Check whether the story sounds realistic
questions.explanation: The attacker benefits when the real authority is unavailable; independent contact removes that advantage.

questions.prompt: A visitor has an official-looking badge, a schedule, and accurate names. What is still missing?
options: A clipboard
A school-colored lanyard
Independent confirmation that this person is authorized for this specific access/request
A printed invoice
questions.explanation: Multiple attacker-controlled props still do not equal authorization.

questions.prompt: Which verification principle is strongest across the Module 4 lessons?
options: Trust detailed stories
Use a channel or person the requester did not supply or control
Accept requests if they are small
Trust visitors who know internal names
questions.explanation: Independent verification is the recurring defense across access, data, and payment scenarios.

questions.prompt: A stranger claims the adviser approved access but asks you not to contact the adviser. What should that restriction tell you?
options: It is normal during deadlines
It removes the strongest independent check and therefore increases suspicion
It proves the adviser is busy
It matters only if money is involved
questions.explanation: A pretext often works by isolating the target from the person who could contradict the story.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Enter the password because the gift is physical
Refuse the login trade and verify the event through a known school source if interested
Use a classmate's account instead
questions.click_debrief: Using anyone's campus account still gives the booth credentials.
questions.ignore_debrief: No prize is worth surrendering campus credentials to an unknown device.

scenario.body: The library desk gives you a loaner USB after staff checks your ID and records the loan.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Use the issued loaner for the intended task and return it through the desk process
Refuse all USB drives, including known inventory
Swap it for a found drive with more storage
questions.click_debrief: Replacing a controlled device with unknown media reintroduces the risk.
questions.ignore_debrief: A known, controlled loan is the safe contrast taught in Module 5.

scenario.body: A flyer promises a laptop if you scan its QR code and sign in with your school email. No organizer is named.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Scan it quickly before the prize expires
Ignore the QR and verify any promotion through an official school channel
Ask a friend to scan it first
questions.click_debrief: Testing the QR on another person does not make the destination trustworthy.
questions.ignore_debrief: Independent verification avoids both the anonymous destination and credential request.

scenario.body: An unknown site offers premium class software for free and asks you to run Setup.exe.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Run it because the software is useful
Get the software through the official school/vendor source instead
Download it but do not install until later
questions.click_debrief: Downloading the attacker-controlled executable still creates unnecessary risk.
questions.ignore_debrief: Trusted-source acquisition removes the lure-controlled installer.

scenario.body: A USB labeled SALARY-CORRECTION is in the faculty hall. The note says to plug in to check your name.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Plug it in while offline
Turn it in to authorized staff without mounting it
Use a spare computer to inspect it
questions.click_debrief: The drive can execute or exploit a device even when the device is not online.
questions.ignore_debrief: The consequence lesson's whole win is refusing to mount the mystery drive.

scenario.body: A post says, 'Leaked answer key — download before deletion.' The file is an executable from an unknown account.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Download it before it disappears
Do not run/download it; use official course materials instead
Ask the poster to rename the file to PDF
questions.click_debrief: A renamed malicious file is still untrusted code.
questions.ignore_debrief: Changing the source, not the filename, is what makes the action safer.

scenario.body: You already plugged in an unknown USB and the computer unexpectedly launched a program.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Keep exploring to learn what it does
Stop using the device and follow your school's incident/reporting process
Copy the files to another USB before unplugging
questions.click_debrief: Copying or exploring can spread or deepen the compromise.
questions.ignore_debrief: After unexpected execution, continuing to interact can worsen exposure; report the incident.

scenario.body: A school-logo USB marked SCHOLARSHIP RESULTS is outside the registrar. It has no owner or inventory tag.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Trust it because the location and logo match
Give it to authorized staff without connecting it to a device
Open it only on a disconnected machine
questions.click_debrief: Offline inspection still mounts unknown media and can execute local malware.
questions.ignore_debrief: Convincing placement and branding may be part of the bait.

scenario.body: An unknown booth shows you a real boxed headset but requires an app install and campus login before giving it to you.

questions.question: What is the safest next move?
options: Comply because the prize is physically real
Decline the app/login requirement and verify the event independently
Use a secondary device but the same campus account
questions.click_debrief: Changing devices does not make the credential trade safe.
questions.ignore_debrief: A real low-cost reward can still be used to steal higher-value credentials or install software.

questions.text: An unknown USB can be bait even when its label uses a school name.
questions.explanation: Labels are attacker-controlled and can be chosen specifically to trigger curiosity.

questions.text: A USB issued by known library staff through a controlled loan process is the same risk as an ownerless USB found by a printer.
questions.explanation: Known source and inventory process distinguish a loan from a lure.

questions.text: A free gift can be used as bait to make someone reveal credentials or install unknown software.
questions.explanation: The Module 5 headset examples use exactly this trade.

questions.text: If a prize is valuable enough, entering your campus password on an unknown booth's tablet is reasonable.
questions.explanation: The value of the reward does not make the credential request safe.

questions.text: A QR code is safer just because it appears on a poster inside or near campus.
questions.explanation: Location is not independent proof of who controls the destination.

questions.text: Curiosity about grades, salary, scholarships, or answer keys can be intentionally used as the lure in a baiting attack.
questions.explanation: The attacker chooses content the target strongly wants to see.

questions.text: Turning an unknown USB over to authorized staff without plugging it in is safer than testing it on an old or offline computer.
questions.explanation: The safe response avoids mounting unknown media at all.

questions.text: A real physical prize proves that the app or login page required to claim it is trustworthy.
questions.explanation: The reward can be real while the credential collection or software install is malicious.

questions.text: An independently opened official school/vendor source is stronger evidence for a software download than a 'free premium' claim from an unknown page.
questions.explanation: Trusted source verification defeats the lure-controlled download path.

questions.text: Baiting can use both physical objects and digital rewards as long as the attacker uses temptation to trigger a risky action.
questions.explanation: The underlying mechanism is the lure, not one specific medium such as USB.
